overview.description: Four-Two-Three (4-2-3) is a Guts-family poker variant. Each player is dealt four cards face-down; players declare in or out simultaneously (e.g. with a coin in fist). The dealer then deals three common cards face up. Players who stayed in form their best five-card poker hand from their four hole cards plus the three board cards; the best hand wins the pot. All who stayed in and lost must match the pot. Game ends when one player stays in alone and wins.

history.origins: Variant of Four-Two-Two (4-2-2), contributed by Brian Johnson; differs by dealing three common cards instead of two face-up cards per player.
timeline: Guts variant with a second deal after the declare; three community cards instead of two per player.
history.cultural: Played as a dealer's choice option in Guts and match-pot poker games.

nullReasons.evolution: No documented evolutionary timeline for this specific variant.

setup.players: Two to ten players; Guts-style games typically work best with around five to ten. All agree ante and optional maximum loss per deal before play.
setup.equipment: Cards, chips or money for ante and pot, optional coin for simultaneous declare.
setup.dealing: Dealer shuffles and deals four cards face-down to each player. After declarations, dealer deals three common cards face up in the center.

rules.objective: Win the pot by having the best five-card poker hand among those who stayed in, or win without contest if you are the only player in.
rules.gameplay: Four cards dealt to each player. Players declare in or out simultaneously (e.g. coin in closed fist; those with a coin are in). Dealer deals three common cards face up. Each player in forms best five-card hand from four hole cards plus three board cards (seven cards total). Best hand wins pot; all others who stayed in match the pot. If only one stays in, that player wins the pot without showing. Game ends when one player wins the whole pot by being the only one in.
keyRules: Four cards each, then simultaneous declare in or out
Three common cards dealt after declare
Best five-card poker hand from seven cards wins
Losers who stayed in each match the pot

strategy.basic: Stay in only with strong four-card hands; avoid matching large pots with marginal hands.
strategy.intermediate: Consider pot size and number of players in when deciding; tight play when pot is large.
strategy.advanced: Balance value and bluff given the single round of declaration and three common cards; exploit opponents who overplay weak four-card hands.
tips: Twos are wild in the related 4-2-2; confirm before play whether 4-2-3 uses wilds.
Agree a maximum loss per deal to cap risk when pot grows large.
